subtopics.title: Subsidence, Convergence and the Rain Switch

questions.question: Converging surface winds produce rain because:
options: The air is forced UP, expands, cools adiabatically, its vapour condenses and cloud and rain follow
Converging air sinks and warms
Convergence dries the air out
The winds cancel each other and the air stops moving

questions.question: A temperature inversion built by subsidence acts as:
options: A source of extra rainfall
A ceiling of warm-above-cold air that stops thermals from rising high enough to form cloud
A trigger for thunderstorms
A cold front

questions.question: The Sahara, Kalahari and Namib deserts all sit:
options: Under the equatorial low
Along the polar front
Under the permanent SUBSIDENCE of the subtropical high-pressure belts near 30 degrees
Under the ITCZ all year

questions.question: The Congo Basin is wet nearly all year because it lies:
options: Next to a cold ocean current
On the polar side of the westerlies
Under the Kalahari High
Under permanent equatorial CONVERGENCE, where rising air makes convectional rain almost daily

subtopics.title: The ITCZ — the Rain Belt That Migrates

questions.question: The ITCZ is best defined as:
options: The low-pressure trough where the south-east and north-east trade winds converge and force air upward on a grand scale
A belt of subsiding air near 30 degrees
The boundary between the westerlies and polar easterlies
A cold ocean current along the equator

questions.question: In January the ITCZ lies:
options: Over the Sahel at about 15 to 20 degrees north
Across southern Africa — roughly over Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe — driving the southern summer rains
Over the Mediterranean
Exactly on the equator, where it stays all year

questions.question: A double rainfall maximum near the equator occurs because:
options: Two cold fronts pass each year
The ocean currents reverse twice a year
The migrating ITCZ crosses those latitudes TWICE a year — once moving north and once moving south
El Niño happens twice a year

questions.question: The ITCZ migrates seasonally because:
options: The Coriolis force reverses with the seasons
The trade winds stop blowing in winter
Ocean tides pull it north and south
It follows the belt of greatest surface heating under the overhead sun, lagging about a month behind it

subtopics.title: The Kalahari High and the Oceans on Either Side

questions.question: The Highveld is dry in winter because:
options: The Kalahari High strengthens and its inversion sinks BELOW the escarpment, shutting moist ocean air off the plateau
The ITCZ sits over Gauteng in winter
The Benguela Current warms up in winter
Cold fronts never reach South Africa in winter

questions.question: In summer the interior receives thunderstorm rain because:
options: The inversion sinks lower in summer
Surface heating weakens the Kalahari High, the inversion lifts ABOVE the escarpment and moist Indian Ocean air floods onto the plateau
The Benguela Current brings moisture from the west
The polar easterlies reach the plateau

questions.question: The Benguela Current keeps the west coast dry because:
options: It is warm and evaporates too quickly
It blocks the trade winds
Its COLD upwelled water chills the air from below, making it stable and nearly moistureless — fog at most, almost never rain
It flows away from the coast

questions.question: Durban is humid and green at the same latitude as dry Port Nolloth because:
options: Durban is at a lower altitude
Durban lies closer to the equator
The Kalahari High covers only the west coast
The warm Mozambique-Agulhas current heats and moistens the east coast air, making it unstable and rain-ready

subtopics.title: Synoptic Charts, Satellites and El Niño

questions.question: On a synoptic chart, a cell labelled H with widely spaced isobars means:
options: An anticyclone — subsiding air, clear settled weather and light winds
A low bringing rain and gales
A cold front
The ITCZ

questions.question: A cold front is drawn on the chart as:
options: A dashed circle around a high
A line of triangles pointing in the direction the front is MOVING, usually sweeping toward the Cape from the south-west
A row of semicircles pointing backwards
A shaded band along the equator

questions.question: On a station model, the wind is read from:
options: The number at upper left
The shading of the circle
A shaft with feathers flying FROM the direction the wind comes from, each full feather worth ten knots
The dew-point figure

questions.question: In an El Niño year, southern Africa usually experiences:
options: Heavier summer rains than normal
No change in weather at all
Colder ocean water off Peru
BELOW-average summer rainfall — the 2015-16 El Niño brought one of the region's worst droughts

questions.question: In the kitchen picture, a pot boiling with the lid OFF stands for:
options: Convergence — air rushing in and shooting up, building cloud and rain
Subsidence and clear skies
A temperature inversion
The Benguela Current

questions.question: The 'lid' pressing down over the Sahara and the Kalahari is:
options: The ITCZ
The subsiding air of the subtropical highs, which stops anything from rising and raining
A cold front that never moves
Dust in the atmosphere

questions.question: A thermal rising from hot ground stops dead at an inversion because:
options: The wind blows it sideways
It runs out of water vapour
It meets a layer of WARMER air above, finds itself cooler and heavier than its surroundings, and can rise no further
The ground stops heating it

subtopics.title: The Sprinkler That Follows the Sun

questions.question: The sprinkler on a north-south rail stands for:
options: The ITCZ sliding up and down the continent as it chases the overhead sun, about a month behind
The Kalahari High
The Benguela Current
The westerlies

questions.question: In July the sprinkler is watering:
options: Zimbabwe and northern South Africa
The Sahel on the southern edge of the Sahara, while southern Africa stands in its dry season
Cape Town
The whole continent at once

questions.question: A place near the far end of the rail, like Zimbabwe or the Sahel, gets:
options: Two rainy seasons a year
Rain all year round
ONE rainy season, because the migrating belt reaches it only once before turning back
No rain in any season

questions.question: When the sprinkler stops short of a district in a given year, the result is:
options: A double rainfall maximum
Flooding
A colder winter
Drought and a failed harvest — most tropical droughts are simply the rain belt not arriving

subtopics.title: Two Buckets and a Weather Map

questions.question: The warm bucket and cold bucket stand for:
options: The warm Mozambique-Agulhas current loading east coast air with moisture, and the cold Benguela leaving west coast air dry and stable
Summer and winter temperatures inland
The two hemispheres
El Niño and the ITCZ

questions.question: The 'lid on a hinge' over the interior describes:
options: A cold front crossing the Cape
The Kalahari High clamping down below the escarpment in winter and lifting above it in summer to let moist air in
The daily sea breeze
The jet stream

questions.question: On the weather map, H and L translate to:
options: Hot and cold places
High and low altitude
H is the lid — sun and no rain; L is the chimney — cloud and rain
Humidity and lightning

questions.question: A news report of La Niña translates, for a South African summer, to:
options: Certain drought
No effect on our weather
A colder winter ahead
Cool Pacific water and usually WETTER summers here — as the flooded summers of 2021 and 2022 showed
